quotes.text: Florence Welch's songwriting captures the essence of poetry.
Her music has always felt so grand and cinematic and was perfect for the kind of kids that were stuck in their own day dreams and fantasies.
With each progressive release, I began to finally appreciate the masterful lyricism alongside the band's fantastic arrangements and production.

The album's guitar work stands out – electric distortion fuels "One of the Greats," while "Sympathy Magic" offers raw acoustic tones. The result bursts with energy. Everybody Scream is her most emotionally descriptive work, pushing creative boundaries.
Florence Welch puts words together in such a unique way. A poetic expression of intense emotional release.

This project feels like one Florence Welch's most moody, heartbreakingly honest records yet. You can palpably feel Welch's pain on tracks like "You Can Have It All" and "Witch Dance," tracks that explore the traumatic events that happened to her over the last few years. While all Florence + The Machine records are pensive, this one in particular took things to a whole new level of brutal honesty.
It leans into everything Florence does best – loud, cathartic bursts like the title track and "Kraken," woven between softer, more intimate moments like "Buckle" and "Sympathy Magic."

Everybody Scream embodies a feminine magic of healing through a range of experiences with pain and self-reliance in relationships and power dynamics, while holding accountability for growth and expression. Dance Fever is an exploration of the healing journey, with vocals that emotionally echo as it pushes through the mundane. Both albums spark a connection with mysticism and soulful narrative.

Everybody Scream is a ritual tapping into raw feminine energy to fight through trauma and find catharsis through a scream. The previous record, Dance Fever acts as almost a precursor utilizing this same energy through dance and song before the primal scream needed to find complete peace.

Welch has long explored the female experience through her own journey, airing passions, private fears, unapologetic ambition, and a lifelong battle with anxiety in songs so sweeping, grandiose and operatic that they take on the quality of myth.

Welch crafts songs that chronicle the contemporary female experience, and at times speak uncannily to what may come. Like some modern-day, musical "Cassandra"—the title of one of Florence + the Machine's best tracks—Welch has often spoken of what she calls the "strange subconscious prescience of songwriting."

The band's signature sound is layered, shimmering, lush and percussive, dominated by Welch's range-defying voice. She sings beautifully, and here and there, for emphasis, slides into a sotto voce speaking voice that explores the boundary between song and poem.
Florence + the Machine's best music, populated by angels, demons and ghouls coming out to play, often verges on the mystical. And what other major band has made the harp a rock 'n' roll essential?

Welch has endured the inevitable comparisons to Kate Bush and Stevie Nicks and a long list of larger-than-life female frontwomen. Yet she's never been shy about also taking her inspiration from men, perhaps most notably the raw power of soul singers like Sam Cooke and Otis Redding, who didn't so much sing as wield their extraordinary voices like moral weapons.
Welch, like Redding, often starts a song tenderly and within minutes builds to something big, bold and emotionally intense.

She sings with her whole body, finding music in movement, and relishes her rapport with the audience. Positively Dionysian in her energy, she stomps to the beat, most often barefoot, drumming on whatever she can lay hands on.

"Everybody Scream," like Florence + the Machine's 2022 "Dance Fever," marks a gradual departure from the band's more raucous and tumultuous early records. Two decades into Welch's storied career she's making music that ponders the demands placed on the female body by performance, the grind of the music industry, and her own ambition, which she fears is at odds with her fluctuating desire for a life more conventional.
That the themes on "Everybody Scream" run darker and more starkly confessional than much of Welch's earlier music makes a sad kind of sense.

The song starts beatific—Welch has long been a fan of chamber music—with a churchy organ, wisping harp and angelic harmonies. Within seconds, though, it devolves into a sultry Welch vocal and a witch choir of shrill, untuned shrieks that make a mockery of harmony, whipping the sound, and our psyches, into a frenzy.
It's music that invites us into a sonic space where song, dance, and, yes, plenty of rage-filled screaming become redemptive.
With its swingy, glam-inspired groove, "Everybody Scream" is at once danceable and sinister, a pact between Florence and the fans she's sacrificed for, and been seduced by.
There's something unabashedly political about a track on which Welch reminds other women, and perhaps herself, that there is more than one way to make meaning in the world.

For much of the record, the tracks steer clear of the lush extravagance of earlier Florence records, struggling to form the anthemic hooks and infectious melodies we know she's capable of, and also mostly missing the witchy vibes the album would appear to be angling towards, all in favour of instead pursuing pretty middle of the road folk arrangements.

The arrangement feels dull and sparse. The rambling, stumbling stream of consciousness style lyrics briefly touching on a number of interesting ideas, before moving on to another tangent. It feels like a lengthy passage of text recited to simple background music, rather than a song written with structure, melody and musicality in mind.

I think these tracks would carry a lot more weight and power had the album been presented as Florence's most personal and stripped back release from the outset, purposefully eschewing big hooks and grand arrangements in favour of something more real and messy.
The album takes what made the band's 2009 debut, "Lungs" a success, Welch's billowy voice laid over disenchanted gospel music, and refines it to the point of near-perfection.
"Ceremonials" is bigger, brighter and filled with more melodrama.
Welch and the band teamed up with producer Paul Epworth, hot off his success with Adele's "21," to create an album filled with polished tracks with hints of R&B, gospel and '60s pop.

Lyrically Welch has grown. On "All this This and Heaven Too," she laments over the fact that she cannot find the words to describe her feelings, but the song is so well-written that the listener has a hard time believing this is true.
She also expands on her own mythos. She further explores her fascination with drowning in the standout track "Never Let Me Go."

The harp is used less on the new album and is only featured heavily on the opening track "Only If for a Night," and used differently in songs such as "Lungs" and "Cosmic Love." The absence of the harp from the foreground of most songs takes "Ceremonials" from their spacey atmosphere and pulls them back down to earth with heavy drum beats, even some that verge on tribal.
Even on slow tempo tracks like "Breaking Down" where Welch's voice is an airy whisper, the track still translates into a howling cry.

The album cover captures the themes of the album well. It features clean lines and an elegant pose of Welch leaning against a mirror, where as the "Lungs" album cover is hectic and disjointed and Welch's lungs are exposed.
